sections.title: The state of Han characters
paragraphs: After Taiwanese Hokkien and Mandarin developed separately over a long period of time, some words in Taiwanese Hokkien are not written with Han characters in Mandarin, while other words do have corresponding Han-character forms in Mandarin but differ in meaning, pronunciation, or usage in Taiwanese Hokkien.

sections.title: Character types used in this dictionary
paragraphs: The character forms used in this dictionary are broadly divided into three types: original characters, semantic-loan characters, and popular or non-standard characters.
orderedItems: Original characters: in contrast to semantic-loan characters, phonetic-loan characters, and newly created characters, these are character forms attested in traditional sources whose meanings are historically related to the Taiwanese Hokkien word. Example: the original character for phang “fragrant” is 〖芳〗, and the original character for sè “small” is 〖細〗.

Semantic-loan characters: a character form with the same meaning is used to represent the Taiwanese Hokkien reading for that meaning. In other words, the shape is borrowed for meaning rather than sound, and the sound used may have another original character. Example: the character 〖人〗 is read jîn in Taiwanese Hokkien, but another word for “person” is lâng, whose original character is written as 〖農〗 or 〖儂〗. This dictionary standardizes 〖人〗 as the written form, so when it is read lâng it is treated as a semantic-loan character. For example, the 人 in 〖人生〗 jîn-sing is an original character, while the 人 in 〖好人〗 hó lâng is a semantic-loan character.
Popular or non-standard characters: non-standard written forms commonly used in society or found in sources.
bullets: Phonetic-loan characters: a Han character is borrowed for its Taiwanese Hokkien pronunciation to write a different word with the same or a similar sound. Example: 〖某〗 is read bóo in Taiwanese Hokkien and can mean “wife”.

Newly created characters: when no usable Han character can be found for either the sound or the meaning, a new character must be created. Most such characters are phono-semantic compounds, with some based on associative meaning. Example: 〖𬦰〗 peh “to climb” is phono-semantic, while 〖躼〗 lò “tall in stature” is associative.

sections.title: Notes on substitute characters
paragraphs: Even when an original character can be identified in traditional sources, this dictionary may still adopt a more easily recognized substitute character in specific cases for the sake of usability and legibility.
orderedItems: When the original form is graphically obscure, extremely rare, and hard for general readers to recognize, a common substitute may be used. Example: “塍” is replaced by “田”.

When different sources preserve multiple written forms and some of them are more common today, the more widely used form is preferred. Example: for lâng, instead of “農／儂”, this dictionary uses “人” as a semantic-loan character.

When a popular form and an original character coexist, and the popular form is easier to recognize, the dictionary may add explanatory notes in the definition. Example: the relationship between “治” and “刣”.

sections.title: Preferred written forms
paragraphs: This dictionary follows Ministry of Education announcements and the dictionary’s current editorial practice, and gives priority to Han-character forms that best balance historical support, phonological correspondence, and recognizability for general readers.
